title: The ravens (1 Kings 17:1–6)
hook: in drought, ravens bring Elijah bread and meat

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kingdom split in two, after setting aside the zekenim. Your line was heed the old counsel. Did you ask someone who has seen the long run? Today, a prophet walks onto the stage with almost no introduction. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

No family tree. No birth story. No call scene. Just a name and a place: Elijah the Tishbite, of the settlers of Gilead. He stands before King Ahab and says there will be no dew or rain in these years, except by his word. Then he leaves. God sends him to hide by a brook near the Jordan, in a land about to go dry. And the food that keeps him alive there comes from a source nobody would have picked. Today's word is the delivery.
screen: `ELIJAH THE TISHBITE.` → `NO DEW OR RAIN.` → `HIDE BY THE BROOK.`

segments.voice: First Kings seventeen. God tells Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, near the Jordan. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." And they do. "And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook." The Hebrew word is orvim, ravens. And ravens, of all birds. In the Torah's list of birds Israel may not eat, the raven is there by name. And here it is carrying bread and meat to a prophet, morning and evening, in a drought. Some later commentators wondered whether orvim might mean people instead of birds. The plain story keeps the birds, and keeps the strangeness. Help arrives on the wings of something the Torah set apart as unfit for the table. There's a quieter point too. Elijah has just spoken a drought into the land. And the very next thing the text shows is that he has to be fed. He doesn't feed himself. He sits by a brook, waits, and accepts food from birds. One way to read it: after his big word, the prophet's next scene is about receiving. And it doesn't last: after a while, the text says, the brook dried up, because there had been no rain. He'll have to move on. But for a time the help came, twice a day, from the last place he'd have looked.
screen: `HIDE BY THE BROOK CHERITH.` · `ORVIM: RAVENS, ON THE TORAH'S LIST.` · `THE PROPHET HAS TO BE FED.` · `THE BROOK DRIES UP.` · then, large: `THE RAVENS BROUGHT HIM BREAD AND FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept help from an unlikely place. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time someone helped you whom you didn't expect: a stranger, a person you had written off, someone you'd kept at arm's length. Let that face come to mind and stay a moment. Then look at today. Is there help being offered that you're refusing because of where it comes from? Pride, suspicion, an old story about that person. If you pray, you can give thanks for the ravens in your life. If you don't, just let the memory stay with you a while. The bell holds the time.
The ravens. Birds on the Torah's list of what not to eat, bringing bread and meat to Elijah by the brook, morning and evening. Today's word.
Your line: the ravens fed him. Today, if help comes from somewhere you didn't expect, say yes before you ask why. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Jews read Elijah's story in the book of Kings, and Elijah appears in Jewish practice beyond it, as in the cup of Elijah set out at the Passover seder.

notes: The view that orvim might mean people (Arabians or men of a town called Orev) is reported in medieval commentary, e.g. Radak; please confirm the citation.
